materials.text:
Reading a p-value: the sleep and memory study

A researcher wants to know whether a short nap helps people remember word lists. Forty students are randomly split into two groups. One group naps for 20 minutes after studying a list of 30 words; the other group sits quietly. The nap group recalls 17.1 words on average and the quiet group recalls 14.9. An independent-samples t-test gives p = .03.

What does p = .03 mean? Start with the null hypothesis: in the population, napping makes no difference to recall. The p-value answers one narrow question. If the null hypothesis were true, how often would random sampling alone produce a difference between groups at least as large as the one we observed? Here the answer is about 3 times in 100. The p-value is therefore a statement about the data, assuming the null hypothesis. It is not a statement about the hypothesis.

This is why p = .03 does not mean there is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true, and it does not mean there is a 97% chance that napping works. To say how probable a hypothesis is, we would need extra information that the test does not use, such as how plausible the effect was before the study.

By convention, a p-value below .05 is called statistically significant, and we reject the null hypothesis. That label says nothing about how big or how important the effect is. With thousands of participants, a trivially small difference can produce a tiny p-value. To judge size, look at the effect size (here the difference is 2.2 words, Cohen's d of about 0.7) and at the 95% confidence interval for the difference (0.2 to 4.2 words), which shows how uncertain the estimate is.

Finally, a p-value above .05 does not prove there is no effect. A small study may simply lack the power to detect a real difference. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Report what you found, how big it was, and how sure you can be.

stakes.text: Jordan writes in the lab report that 'there is only a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true, so napping definitely improves memory a lot'. The marker takes marks off for misinterpreting the test, and Jordan goes on repeating the mistake in their final-year project

preparation.briefing:
Purpose: Practise explaining, in plain words, what a p-value from a two-group study does and does not tell you.
Your role: Your classmate Jordan missed the lecture on the sleep-and-memory study (nap group 17.1 words, quiet group 14.9 words, p = .03) and has a lab report due tomorrow. Help Jordan understand what the result really means, correct anything Jordan gets wrong, and say what else they should look at before deciding whether the nap effect matters.
You will talk to Jordan, who is confident and will push back until your explanation actually makes sense.
Keep in mind: no formulas or calculations are needed. Use the nap study as your example and the material below to check yourself.

turns.text: Before you start: in one sentence, what do you think p = .03 tells you about the nap study?
It means there is only a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true, so we can be about 97% sure that napping really does improve recall.
Apart from the p-value, what else would you want to know before saying napping 'works'?
I would want to know if the sample was big enough and whether the groups were randomly assigned. Honestly though, a p that low already tells me the effect is pretty solid.

Hi, I'm Jordan. I missed the stats lecture and I have to write up the nap study by tomorrow. The output says p = .03. I was going to write 'there's only a 3% chance the result is a fluke', but someone said that's not quite right.
So what does p = .03 actually mean? What is the 3% a percentage of?

It's basically what your friend said but stronger: p = .03 means there's only a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true. So there's a 97% chance napping really does help memory, which is why we call it significant.

Hold on. You said something that sounded like "there's only a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true, so a 97% chance that napping really works". If that were true, what would we expect to see? Does that match what you know?
I'm not totally sure what you mean by what we'd expect to see. I mean, if there's a 97% chance it works, we'd expect the nap group to remember more, and they did, 17.1 vs 14.9. So yeah it matches?
I don't know any more than that, sorry. What do you think?

OK so imagine another study got p = .001. That would mean only a 0.1% chance the null is true, so the effect is way more certain and probably a lot bigger than the nap effect. Smaller p, stronger effect basically.
I'm not sure I follow yet. Can you say a bit more, maybe with an example?

Wait, I never said anything about p above .05 proving napping does nothing. But yes, I do think smaller p means a bigger effect, because a really big difference between groups is what makes the p tiny. I'm not sure what else we'd expect to see.
Maybe look back at the course material from before we started. Is there a part of it that helps here?

OK, I just reread it and it literally says p = .03 does NOT mean a 3% chance the null is true. It's more like: if napping did nothing, you'd only get a gap of 2.2 words or bigger about 3 times in 100 just by chance. So the 3% is about the data assuming the null, not about the null itself. I had that backwards.
Okay, I think I follow. But suppose someone disagreed with you. What would you say to convince them?

I'd say the test starts by assuming napping does nothing, so it can't turn around and tell you how likely that assumption is. To get a chance that napping works you'd need extra info, like how believable it was before the study. But I still think the low p shows the nap effect is fairly big, that part hasn't changed for me.
Fine, but .03 is a really small number, so the nap effect must be huge, right? Can I write that napping has a big effect on memory?

Because the whole calculation is done in a world where napping does nothing. It tells you how surprising our 2.2-word gap would be in that world, not how likely that world is. It's like asking how often you'd get 8 heads out of 10 with a fair coin, which isn't the same as the chance the coin is fair.
I'm not sure I follow yet. Can you say a bit more, maybe with an example?

I literally just gave you the coin example. Anyway, for your report I'd write that p = .03 means a 2.2-word gap would be unusual if naps did nothing, so the result is significant. And since .03 is pretty small, you can say the nap effect is a big, important one.
Could you put that in one sentence I could write down?

You already asked me that one, Jordan. Short version: the test assumes naps do nothing and asks how weird our data would be, so it can't also tell you the chance that naps do nothing. Did you have a question about the size of the effect?
Sorry, you're right, you did. Let's move on.
And if it had come out as p = .20, I'd just write that napping does nothing, yeah?

Hm, the bit about size says that with thousands of people even a tiny difference can get a tiny p. So I guess p mixes up how big the effect is with how many people you tested, and a smaller p doesn't automatically mean a bigger effect. For size you'd look at the 2.2 words, Cohen's d of about 0.7, and the confidence interval of 0.2 to 4.2, which is pretty wide.
Oh, that's useful, it answers something I was going to ask. And if it had come out as p = .20, I'd just write that napping does nothing, yeah?
Thank you. I think I could explain some of this to someone else now.
Before you see any feedback: how do you think that went? Which moment are you most satisfied with?

Mixed. I started off telling Jordan the exact wrong thing about the 3%, but I'm happiest with the coin example, because that's when I actually understood why the p-value can't be the chance the null is true.
What would you do differently if you did it again?

I'd read the course material properly before starting instead of being so sure of myself, and I'd talk about effect size and the confidence interval from the start instead of saying a small p means a big effect. Jordan also kept asking the same question, which got frustrating.

A different situation: a newspaper headline says a new revision app 'significantly improves exam scores (p = .04)' in a study of 6,000 pupils, and a friend asks whether they should pay for it. What from this session would you use there, and what would you change?

I'd tell them p = .04 doesn't mean a 96% chance the app works, it just means the result would be unusual if the app did nothing. And with 6,000 pupils even a tiny improvement can come out significant, so I'd want to know how many marks it actually adds and the confidence interval before paying for it.
